context: letters from J. D. Hooker, which you are answering
exchanges:
Our only large Flagellaria is 40 years old,! & we fear to remove it. Yours of Feby 6 is most intensely interesting & suggestive— What gigantic strides you are making in Veg. Phys.— Bentham is most anxious to have something this of yours to allude to in his anniversary address at which he is working

We have not Naravelia alive, but I am writing to Anderson at Calcutta about it.— I do not see how we can any longer deny nerve-force to plants;— I think we used once to argue about it— When & where do you propose to publish?

I suppose axis may pass into tendrils somehow as any organ may become axial & bear buds.

Poor Horner has been at deaths-door with congestion of Lungs, last Friday or Saturday but is much better. he is in his 80th. year I think. All the family are up. Lyell came & spent Sunday afternoon & evening with us, very pleasantly, full of chat; we discussed Franklands new glacial theory which I think the most monstrous absurdity ever broached in Science & the most ill digested attempt. Have you seen Falconers attempt to explain absence of Lakes in Himal Valleys?— I fear it is not very successful.

Have you seen the pamphlet on the production of sexes in animals &c, if not I can send it you.

In “Ansted Ionian Islands” is a very suggestive account of the way vegetation breaks up rocks, & buildings producing Earthquaque appearances.

I saw Lindley on Sunday looking very ill, complaining of constant headaches with the loss of memory.— So poor old Portlock is gathered to his fathers.

I am very glad of the settlement of the Williams case by the Privy Council—& shall subscribe to the Colenso defence fund on principle; but am not quite sure about Colenso himself— he ought to go further. My hope is that after the trial he will go out just to assert his position & then retire. his holding his Bishopric in Natal can only breed intolerable confusion & do his cause mischief; & as to his going out to convert Zulus, why, he has Xtians here to convert, & the Zulus are not worth a thought:— He might come back with great glory & set up in England as a Tutor abandoning his title & mitre. I have seen a good deal of him & consider him sanguine & unsafe.

We are making private enquiries about a Curator to succeed Mr Smith, & I have written to Balfour, I wonder if he will recommend Scott; if he wants to get rid of him he is sure to do so. Do you know any-thing of Scotts capacity as manager of a large establishment, with 5 foremen, & no end of accounts, gardeners & labourers under him. I have my eye on the D. of Northumberlands Gardener at Syon, a man I like much, who had the wit to impregnate the Cocoa-nut which is now ripening & is very fond of scientific gardening, keeps an enormous establishment in splendid order, & is not too old.— oddly enough his name is John Smith.! he has been to volunteer for the appointment but we have taken no steps whatever yet.

Ever yr affec | J D Hooker

I send the only two Corydalis we have of the things you mentioned   I doubt the Tourrettia being in cultivation now, I never saw it. The Sikkim Corydalis is a large growing much branched rambling species, which I should think should be raised in a green house & then planted out amongst shrubs in a good soil. I found it always always scrambling over shrubs on the verge of the forest.

How I wish you would get well.

Ever yr affec | J D Hooker.

Crugers seems to be a splendid paper— how I wish he were a better Botanic Gardener— he has been instructed to propagate Cinchona in Trinidad, & made a regular mess of it.— A German scientific man is the most impractical & impracticable pig in Christendom.

I have two letters from you full of interesting news to me.— In your former one you tell me about H. C. Watson: I never heard anything like it; why the man must be insane with ill-humour.— Pray tell me when the article appears, for it will be a literary curiosity.

I know nothing of Scott’s fitness for your most arduous post of head-man; what a responsibility you must feel on subject.— If you read Scot’s paper & can say a word of praise or criticism do let me hear, for I am sure he wd. value your praise especially.— I am delighted about making him an associate; I have no doubt it will stimulate him to good work.—

I shd. like to know, if you can remember, who wrote in G. Chron. the nice notice of poor Boott.— Who reviewed Lyell in Quarterly; I ask the latter out of mere idle curiosity.—

In your last you allude to Frankland’s paper on Glaciers; I had intended exploding on same subject: it is absurd & I am the more bound to say so, as a former warm sea would never suit the Algæ, Crustacean & Fish common to the N. & S. It amused me to see how coolly he assumed that whole world was cooler during glacial period. I wish I had published my evidence in full on this head.—

I have sent you scraps, asking about seeds of climbing Fumariæ &c— I wish I could get seed of such Fumariæ.— I fear you greatly overrate the interest of my facts on climbing. Pray thank Bentham sincerely for wishing to notice anything of mine; but I could not draw up a paper to save my life.— You ask about my sickness—it rarely comes on till 2–3 hours after eating, so that I seldom throw up food, only acid & morbid secretion; otherwise I shd. have been dead, for during more than a month I vomited after every meal & several times most nights.— On my well days I am certainly stronger— You may know how often I feel well, for I always then give myself the treat of writing to you.—

A. DeCandolle sent me the pamphlet on sexes, which stretches my belief to cracking point.— I do not believe in Falconer’s lakes.— Crügers letter has stirred me up about Orchids, & I skimmed over my Chaptr. on Catesidæ, & I can now look impartially at the case, & I declare the structure & action of Catasetum, is, as it seems to me, about the oddest case in vegetable Kingdom.— If Cryptopodium ever flowers at Kew, I shd. much like to see it; I have 2 plants, but they will not flower; I have seen all other genera of Catasetidæ.— I enclose scraps, which will not cause much trouble to answer, about climbers, & a few more requests; pray observe you owe this to yourself, as your interest on subject has stimulated me.—

Since first part of letter was written, I have received seeds of Corydalis &c— Most cordial thanks.— I am tired.—

Yours affectionately | C. Darwin

Feb. 22d
